Power of the Two One-Sided Tests Procedure (TOST) for Equivalence

Source: R/power_equivalence_md.R
power_equivalence_md.Rd

Computes the power of the Schuirmann (1987) two one-sided tests procedure , the probability that a \((1 - 2\alpha)\) confidence interval for the mean difference (or ratio, on the log scale) lies entirely within the equivalence interval \([\theta_1, \theta_2]\) (lower_bound and upper_bound), by numerical integration over the chi distribution of the sample standard deviation.

Usage

power_equivalence_md(
  alpha_level,
  logscale,
  lower_bound,
  upper_bound,
  true_effect,
  true_sd,
  n_per_treatment,
  df_error
)

Arguments

alpha_level

Type I error rate for each of the two one-sided tests (typically 0.05). The full equivalence test uses a \((1 - 2\alpha)\) confidence interval.

logscale

Logical. If TRUE, treatment means are compared on the logarithmic scale; lower_bound, upper_bound, and true_effect are then given as ratios of test to reference on the original scale (untransformed) and are log-transformed internally. If FALSE, they are differences of the means.

lower_bound

Lower limit of the equivalence interval on the original scale: a ratio when logscale = TRUE (logged internally), a difference otherwise.

upper_bound

Upper limit of the equivalence interval on the original scale: a ratio when logscale = TRUE (logged internally), a difference otherwise.

true_effect

The true (population) effect: the ratio of the treatment means on the original scale when logscale = TRUE (logged internally), the difference in treatment means otherwise.

true_sd

\(\sqrt{\mathrm{error\ variance}}\); root-MSE from an ANOVA. On the log scale, this is the coefficient of variation.

n_per_treatment

Number of subjects who receive each treatment: the size of each group in a parallel design, and the number of subjects in a crossover design, where every subject receives both treatments. It is the same quantity in both designs, the \(n\) of the standard error \(\sigma \sqrt{2 / n}\) of the estimated difference, so in a parallel design it is the size of one group and never the total. Must be greater than 1.

df_error

Error degrees of freedom associated with true_sd.

Value

A one-row data.frame with columns term ("power") and value (the computed power, in \([0, 1]\)).

Details

The computation conditions on the error standard deviation the study will actually observe. Given that value, whether the confidence interval fits inside the equivalence interval is an ordinary normal probability, and the power is that probability averaged over the chi distribution the error standard deviation follows on df_error degrees of freedom. The averaging is carried out on a unit-free scale, with the equivalence limits expressed in standard errors and the error standard deviation as a multiple of true_sd, so the power depends on the design rather than on the units of the response: with logscale = FALSE, multiplying lower_bound, upper_bound, true_effect, and true_sd by a common factor leaves the answer unchanged.

The scale of the bounds and the true effect. This function and power_equivalence_md_plot take lower_bound, upper_bound, and true_effect on the original scale: ratios of test to reference with logscale = TRUE, which are logged before the computation, and differences with logscale = FALSE, which are used as given. power_density_equivalence_md takes them on the analysis scale and transforms nothing, so power_equivalence_md(logscale = TRUE, lower_bound = .8, ...) corresponds to power_density_equivalence_md(lower_bound = log(.8), ...).

For Phillips's (1990) original example (regular-scale two-period crossover with \(\theta_1 = -0.2\), \(\theta_2 = 0.2\), CV \(= 0.20\), \(\delta = 0.05\), \(n = 24\), \(\nu = 22\), which are lower_bound, upper_bound, true_sd, true_effect, n_per_treatment, and df_error), this function reproduces the published value of \(0.8029678\) (Phillips, 1990, Table 1, 5th row, 5th column).

Note

See the legacy MBESS package (Kelley, 2007a, 2007b) for additional details and discussion.

References

Diletti, E., Hauschke, D., & Steinijans, V. W. (1991). Sample size determination of bioequivalence assessment by means of confidence intervals. International Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, Therapy and Toxicology, 29(1), 1–8.

Kelley, K. (2007a). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K. (2007b). Methods for the behavioral, educational, and social sciences: An R package. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 979–984. doi:10.3758/BF03192993

Phillips, K. F. (1990). Power of the two one-sided tests procedure in bioequivalence. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 18(2), 137–144. doi:10.1007/BF01063556

Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). A comparison of the two one-sided tests procedure and the power approach for assessing the equivalence of average bioavailability. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 15(6), 657–680.

power_equivalence_md_plot, power_density_equivalence_md

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Table 1 of Phillips, 1990, fifth row and fifth column, where the
# published power is 0.8029678.
power_equivalence_md(alpha_level = .05, logscale = FALSE,
                     lower_bound = -.2, upper_bound = .2,
                     true_effect = .05, true_sd = .20,
                     n_per_treatment = 24, df_error = 22)
#>  term  value
#>  power 0.803

# Table 1 of Diletti et al., 1991, on the log scale, so the limits and
# the true difference are ratios of test to reference. The published
# power is 0.7922796.
power_equivalence_md(alpha_level = .05, logscale = TRUE,
                     lower_bound = .8, upper_bound = 1.25,
                     true_effect = 1.05, true_sd = .20,
                     n_per_treatment = 18, df_error = 16)
#>  term  value
#>  power 0.792
